storylines.label: Retrieval Execution
storylines.latest_title: EPGM: Execution Provenance for Budgeted Agent Memory Retrieval

prior_narrative.tldr: Oct 6 and Oct 9 papers studied how agents pick skills and tools: one optimizes skill injections to survive routers, the other adds execution-time reliability to tool retrieval. The common thread is that agent retrieval is judged on what happens at execution, not only on semantic match.
prior_narrative.whats_new: EPGM, posted Oct 17, applies the execution lens to agent memory: it adds execution provenance to budgeted memory retrieval.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Three independent papers treat retrieval for skills, tools, and memory as an execution-time reliability problem. Relevance-only retrieval in an agent stack can pick items that are unavailable or unsafe at run time.

status.detail: Three papers on skill, tool, and memory retrieval, each tied to execution behavior; none is a shipped product.

beats.headline: Skill-router paper optimizes skill injections for retrieval and execution
beats.summary: Covers third-party skills selected dynamically by skill routers.

beats.headline: RATED adds tool availability during execution to tool retrieval
beats.summary: Targets methods that optimize semantic relevance but ignore execution-time availability.

beats.headline: EPGM brings execution provenance to budgeted agent memory retrieval

open_questions: Do any of the three papers report results on a public agent benchmark that others can reproduce?
Does any skill router or tool-retrieval library adopt execution-aware scoring?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If your agent retrieves tools or skills by embedding similarity alone, log whether each retrieved item was actually available and succeeded at run time, so you can measure the gap these papers target.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: Trapped in Your Story: Evaluating Narrative-Induced Sycophancy in Large Language Models

prior_narrative.tldr: This page groups three arXiv papers by the shared phrase "large language models" in their titles; they do not form one developing story. They cover hidden-state hallucination detection (Oct 1), a security attack on speculative decoding (Oct 6), and narrative-induced sycophancy (Oct 16).
prior_narrative.whats_new: Oct 16 adds an arXiv study showing that LLMs shift toward a user's view when the user justifies it with a personal narrative, widening sycophancy testing beyond bare opinions.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Each paper names a distinct failure surface: hallucination probing needs access to hidden states, speculative decoding adds a draft-model attack path, and sycophancy skews answers in user-facing agents. Treat them as three separate checks, not one trend.

beats.headline: Cross-model span-level hallucination detection probes hidden states
Secure speculative decoding targets the draft-model path in LLM inference
Narrative-induced sycophancy evaluated in LLMs

open_questions: Do hidden-state hallucination probes transfer across model families without per-model training?
Does the speculative-decoding defense add measurable latency over unprotected drafting?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Do not cite these three papers as corroborating each other; if you run user-facing agents, add a sycophancy case where the user justifies a wrong claim with a personal story, and judge the other two papers separately.

prior_narrative.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of RL items, not one developing story. Since Oct 1 it has collected a privacy-constrained RL paper, a Qwen long-horizon agent approach, and an O-RAN benchmark.

storylines.label: Alibaba's Qwen-Image-2.1 open-weight launch
storylines.latest_title: Qwen Image: Every Release, Which to Use, and the 2.5 Gap

prior_narrative.tldr: Alibaba's Qwen team released Qwen-Image-2.1, a 7B open-weight image generation and editing model, in late September; by Oct 7 a hands-on guide covered LoRA fine-tuning for product images. On Oct 9 the eight-step Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo landed on Hugging Face with a license caveat.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Oct 13: an OrcaRouter guide catalogs every Qwen Image release, says which to use, and flags a gap where a 2.5 release would sit.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: An eight-step Turbo variant of a 7B image model cuts per-image latency and GPU cost for self-hosted pipelines, but the license decides whether it can ship commercially.

open_questions: Does the Turbo license permit commercial use, given the base weights were reported as research-use only?
Does eight-step Turbo hold output quality against the base model on independent evals?
Do LoRA fine-tunes of the 7B model hold quality on product imagery beyond one walkthrough?
Will Alibaba ship a Qwen Image 2.5 release, and under what license?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Confirm the license for both base and Turbo weights before any commercial use, then compare eight-step Turbo output against base Qwen-Image-2.1 on your own eval set for quality and latency.

storylines.label: Jev TypeSafe
storylines.latest_title: [AINews] TypeSafe/Jev at >$100M ARR, $7.5B valuation 3 weeks after launch

prior_narrative.tldr: TypeSafe AI launched Jev as a decision-only "System One" model that classifies, routes, and scores, claiming over 100x the speed and 200x the cost efficiency of small frontier LLMs. LangChain published an integration guide and InfoQ described its typed-probability output.
prior_narrative.whats_new: AINews reported Oct 10 that TypeSafe/Jev passed $100M ARR at a $7.5B valuation three weeks after launch; the figures are the newsletter's headline claim, not an audited disclosure.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: A purpose-built model that's 100x faster and 200x cheaper than a small frontier LLM is a strong fit for the classify/route/score steps buried inside most agent pipelines — the exact spots teams currently overpay a general-purpose LLM to handle.

beats.headline: LangChain documents Jev's place in the agent loop
beats.summary: A first-party guide to TypeSafe AI's "System One" model moves Jev from announcement to wiring instructions.

beats.headline: InfoQ: Jev returns typed probabilities, not text
beats.summary: Output is a structured decision with typed probabilities, which is what makes it droppable into classify/route/score steps.

beats.headline: Reported >$100M ARR and $7.5B valuation three weeks after launch
beats.summary: Commercial traction is claimed in a newsletter headline; the underlying figures are not yet independently sourced here.

open_questions: Do Jev's speed/cost claims hold up against a real agent pipeline's classify/route/score calls, not just TypeSafe's own benchmarks?
Will other labs ship a comparable decision-model category, or does this stay a single-vendor niche?
Do typed probabilities from Jev stay calibrated on a team's own routing labels, not just TypeSafe's evaluation sets?
Do TypeSafe or an independent source confirm the >$100M ARR and $7.5B valuation figures?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If a general-purpose LLM call in your agent pipeline only classifies, routes, or scores, benchmark Jev against it on your own labels; treat the ARR and valuation reports as adoption signal, not performance evidence.
